title: Andrew Watson on Handwriting vs. Laptops: Research Keeps Shifting the Goalposts
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio publishes Andrew Watson's update on the claim that handwriting beats laptops for learning. Watson uses a comic dialogue to show how supporters keep moving the goalposts: from remembering more, to brain activity, to a study of 36 participants writing fifteen words with a stylus or one typing finger. He points out that the key EEG study never measured learning or memory, and cites a published rebuttal calling its conclusions a logical shortcut from college students in a lab to children in a classroom. Watson says he is not claiming laptops are better, only that the research does not yet support a research-based claim for handwriting. His wider worry is non-teachers using neuroscience to boss teachers around.
points: The headline study measured brain connectivity, not learning, so it cannot support the claim that handwriting improves memory or learning.
The experiment's artificial setup, writing fifteen words versus one-finger typing, limits how far results generalise to real note-taking.
Another set of scholars published a rebuttal in the same journal calling the extrapolation to classroom learning slippery at best.
Watson's position is a demand for evidence that directly measures the claim, not a claim that laptops are superior.
He cautions that research should be held to its limits when used to direct teachers.
quotes: The researchers did not measure how much the students learned/remembered. Honestly. No quiz. No brain dump. Nothing.
Imagine that I claimed “research shows that this drug will lower your blood pressure!” but I never actually measured anyone’s blood pressure. This study takes a similar logical shortcut.
So, these 36 participants wrote the same fifteen words multiple times. Sometimes they wrote with a stylus on a tablet; sometimes they typed using only their right index finger.
They share my alarm that research which never measured any learning is being used to make strong claims about learning.
If I say to you: “Research shows that handwriting is better for learning than laptops,” I should be able to show you research that directly measures that claim.
Over and over, I find that non-teachers cite research—especially neuroscience research—to boss teachers around.
